messages.subject: DS - questions on CDS model
parts:
Hello,
 
For a study on passerines in a limited perimeter, we used “Point transect” and “radial distance”. In the DS 6.2 software, we took the analysis  engine “CDS”, first with default parameter and then with the five others models (see the results below for Dunnock).
 
What is the best model ? the one with the lowest AIC ? even if  the confidence interval is large ?
 
If a warning is present, what about the value of the result ?
 
Is the size of the interval confidence a selection criterion ? 

Thanks in advance.

Best regards,

Gilles S.

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DS - questions on CDS model
parts:
Giles

Taking your questions in random order:  warnings do not necessarily mean there are problems with the analysis--warnings indicate have a look at the output to see if there is anything amiss.

I suspect there is an error in one of the last two lines of your table.  If two models have the same AIC and the same confidence intervals, they should have the same estimate of abundance (982 vs 932).

For your central question regarding how to select the most appropriate model:  AIC will rank amongst competing models; we call AIC a "relative" measure of fit.  AIC measures the performance of models relative to one another, another step is needed to determine whether models with low AIC values actually fit the observed data.  In addition to using AIC and goodness of fit measures, you will also use your understanding of the habitat and the species you are studying.  These statistics serve as guides--if the rules regarding model selection were absolute, we would program the rules into Distance and have the programme produce the 'correct' answer.  There remains some 'art' to the model selection process.

You would also want to include an absolute measure of fit--namely a goodness of fit test.  If you have analysed exact distances, Distance will produce Kolomogorov-Smirnov (K-S) and Cramer-von Mises (CvM) tests of fit.  You should use models that fit the detection data.  For point transect data, Distance produces two different plots, the g(x) plots (you have shown) and the "pdf" plots.  It is the pdf plots that give a better indication of the fit of the models to your data (along with the K-S/CvM test results).

Finally, confidence interval size should *not* be used to select a model.  Choosing a model with a small confidence interval heightens the chance that the true abundance of the population does not fall within that small confidence interval.

The challenge with the data you show is the large number of detections in the first histogram interval (I cannot read the width of that bin).  Given these birds are often on the ground under cover, I would have thought they would be hard to detect at close distances.  You might want to re-examine the data with smaller bin widths and perhaps truncate more of your data where there are few detections at large distances.  You are getting a discrepancy in abundance estimates because some models are trying to fit that spike at small distances (hazard rate models) and other models (uniform with adjustments) are not trying to fit the spike.  The central question in your analysis is whether that spike is real or an artefact of the manner in which the histograms are created.  Only those who collected the data can answer that question.
